hints: Focus on what the word formation really means, making one mole of the compound starting only from its elements.
Check the standard states of the elements, carbon is a solid graphite and hydrogen exists as $\text{H}_2(g)$, not as single atoms.
Now look at the product, one mole of propane in the state it naturally exists in under standard conditions, and see which equation matches all three rules.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of standard enthalpy of formation**

Great start, let us remember the rule together. It is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states.

Definition rule:
$$1 \text{ mole compound from elements (standard states)} \rightarrow \Delta H_f^\ominus$$

**Check the reactants must be elements in standard states**

Propane is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$, so we need only C and H as reactants. Carbon standard state is solid graphite, $\text{C(s)}$, not $\text{C(g)}$. Hydrogen standard state is diatomic gas, $\text{H}_2\text{(g)}$, not $\text{H(g)}$.

**Check the product amount and state**

We must make exactly 1 mole of propane. Under standard conditions propane is a gas, so we need $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{(g)}$, not liquid.

Correct formation equation:
$$3\text{C(s)} + 4\text{H}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{(g)}$$

**Match to the options**

Only one equation has solid carbon, hydrogen gas, and one mole of gaseous propane in the correct ratio. That is the definition of $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ for propane.

options.A: Incorrect because carbon is shown as $\text{C(g)}$. The standard state of carbon is solid graphite, $\text{C(s)}$, so this does not represent formation from standard states.
options.B: Incorrect because both elements are shown as gaseous atoms, $\text{C(g)}$ and $\text{H(g)}$. Standard states are $\text{C(s)}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{(g)}$, so this is atomisation plus formation, not just formation.
options.C: Correct because 1 mole of $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{(g)}$ is formed from its elements in their standard states, $3\text{C(s)} + 4\text{H}_2\text{(g)}$. This matches the definition of standard enthalpy of formation exactly.
options.D: Incorrect because the product is shown as $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{(l)}$. Propane is a gas under standard conditions, so the standard enthalpy of formation must produce $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8\text{(g)}$.
